source.facts: Confirmed by Winston (Nov 27 2026, ANSWERS.md, Garden): Sun Life uXperience Design Jam, November 2, 2024 (University of Waterloo Stratford School news article; PDF schedule: one day, 6.5 hours working time, 3-minute presentations). Team of six (slide 558:7010): Gaurav Shah, Emily Chan, Charlene Lee, Winston Zhao, Darren Millar and Andrew Ellyatt. No award, so no Result row and no placing. Winston designed the app screens and the basic design system (not the tree and flower art, the slides, the Bento or the banner). The HMW is Sun Life’s prompt, word for word. Deliverables: clickable prototype and live pitch. The three rougher home screens are his earlier versions. Garden is its own app that links people to Sun Life products and advisors. Lessons he chose: pitch it as a story; make progress visible. Everything else is read from the PDF (brief, workshops, Sarah’s story, the four-part concept, the whiteboard) and the screens (text quoted as it appears).

fields.description: Savings plans that bloom as you reach each goal.
fields.intro: Garden is a money app for young Canadians: tell it what you’re saving for, and it builds a plan of small steps and grows flowers and trees as you go. In a team of six at the Sun Life uXperience Design Jam 2024, I designed the app screens and a basic design system.
fields.summary: Designing a savings app that breaks big money goals into small steps and grows a garden as you reach them.
fields.overview: Garden is for young Canadians like Sarah, a busy student saving for her first car. Our team of six designed it in one day at the Sun Life uXperience Design Jam, and we presented it as Sarah’s story in a three-minute live pitch.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.heading: How might we help young Canadians find, and use the financial tools & education available to them?
content: This was Sun Life’s prompt at the uXperience Design Jam, held at the University of Waterloo’s Stratford School on November 2, 2024. Six of us had about six and a half hours to answer it, with a three-minute pitch at the end.

Sun Life’s brief was simple: there are financial tools and education to help young people make money decisions and plan for their goals, but they’re under-used. They asked for something easy and inclusive that helps young Canadians open up about money and feel confident about their financial future.
There were also two workshops that morning: one on financial fluency and one on breaking down barriers with behavioural economics.

sections.title: Persona
sections.heading: Meet Sarah
content: We told the whole pitch through one person. Sarah is a second-year GBDA student at Waterloo with a long commute to Stratford, so she wants a car, but the $2,000 down payment feels like a mountain.

content.caption: Everything competing for Sarah’s time, from our pitch.

content: Between five courses, a part-time job and her friends, money planning keeps getting pushed back. She has never saved this much before and doesn’t know where to start. A chequing account? A high-interest savings account?

sections.title: Idea
sections.heading: Big goals, small steps
content: Before any screens, there was a whiteboard. Around Sun Life’s question, we listed why young people don’t use financial tools: the time it takes, fear, procrastination and relying on parents. Then came the functions we wanted, visual ideas and the problems to design for.

content.alt: A whiteboard covered in red marker: Sun Life’s How might we question at the top, then Why not?, Functions, Visual components, a script outline for Sarah, a Growth column (start with a sapling, plant a tree, grow your own forest), Problems, Gamification and Constraints with AI generated advice
content.caption: Our whiteboard from the day.
The problems we listed, from the whiteboard.

content: The idea we landed on was Garden. It takes one big goal and breaks it into small steps you can act on:

bullets: **Make a plan** from a goal, in your own words.
**Keep track** of your progress as you save.
**Find resources** for each step: answers in the app, outside resources and a financial advisor.
**Act on the plan** in the app, like saving into a new account.

content: Progress shows up as a garden. Smaller goals grow flowers. Saving and learning grow trees, and when your virtual tree is fully grown, a real one gets planted. Garden is its own app, and it points people to Sun Life’s products and advisors along the way.

content.alt: An iPhone showing Garden’s first home screen: Hello, Sarah; Welcome to your Garden with Create a plan, Find resources and Earn badges; and About your Garden, explaining Trees (a real tree is planted after your virtual tree is grown) and Flowers for smaller goals
content.caption: Before the first plan, Home explains how the garden works.

sections.title: Plan
sections.heading: Planning by chat
content: Creating a plan feels like a chat. Garden asks you to write what you want to do, with examples like saving up for a car or paying off student loans.

Sarah types “I need to save $2000 for a car”. Before it plans anything, Garden asks about three things: her timeline, her income and her saving style. She answers, and Garden lays out a Car Savings Plan: $500 every three months, $2,000 over 12 months.

content.alt: Three iPhones with arrows: Create a plan with example goals; Sarah’s message “I need to save $2000 for a car” and Garden asking about Timeline, Your income and Saving style; then the Car Savings Plan with four $500 steps from November 2024 to November 2025, March open with its explanation, and Save and activate plan
content.caption: From a goal to a plan in two messages.

content: Each step opens to explain itself, like why it’s $500 every three months, and the Save and activate plan button turns it on. In our pitch, Sarah’s first steps take minutes: open a high-interest savings account, link it to Garden and set up automatic transfers.

sections.title: Garden
sections.heading: Watch it grow
content: Every plan lives in the Plans tab. Big plans get cards with their total, the next goal and a plant that grows with them. Smaller ones, like a MacBook Pro or a Mexico trip, sit in a list, each with a flower at its own stage.
A toggle at the top switches Plans to Garden, where everything you’ve grown is planted together. Sarah’s garden starts with two flowers and fills in as she finishes goals.

content.alt: Three iPhones with arrows: the Plans tab with cards for Buy Car, Buy House, Retirement Plan and Student Loans, a list of smaller plans (MacBook Pro, Mexico Trip, New Tattoo), each with a flower at its stage, and a New button; the Garden view with two yellow flowers; and the Garden view with a big green tree, a yellow tulip, a sunflower and sprouts
content.caption: Plans, then the garden as it grows.

sections.title: Home
sections.heading: Hello, Sarah
content: Each time Sarah opens Garden, she lands on Home. It leads with a pinned goal, then recent plans with their progress and the badges she has earned, like 500 Saver and 1k Saver.

Home went through three rougher versions before the final one, and two of them are shown here. One had a goal card and plain progress bars for every plan. Another showed plans as dotted timelines with a plant icon at the end, with an Ask button next to the tabs. The final home added the flower on the goal card, badges and a Search tab.

content.alt: Three iPhones with arrows: an early home with a New MacBook Pro card and plain progress bars for Retirement and Student Loan; another early version with Plans as dotted timelines ending in plant icons and an Ask button; and the final home with a sunflower on the goal card, Recent Plans, earned badges and a Search tab
content.caption: Two earlier versions of Home, then the final one.

sections.title: Learn
sections.heading: Resources and search
content: Garden teaches as well as tracks. Resources holds knowledge cards on topics like OSAP loans, GICs, savings and buying a car, each with its own minigames. A list below covers leasing a house, mutual funds and retirement.

Search takes questions in plain words, like “How do I open a savings account?” Its answers come from Garden’s resource bank, and a note under the questions says Search doesn’t generate new data or store yours.

content.alt: Two iPhones: Resources with Search Knowledge Cards, cards for OSAP Loans, What is a GIC?, Savings and Buying a Car with their minigame counts, and a list of Leasing a house, Mutual Funds and Retirement; and Search with How can we help?, three suggested questions and a note that Garden Search answers from a resource bank

sections.title: Nudges
sections.heading: A nudge at the right time
content: Garden also reaches Sarah outside the app. In our pitch, two years after her car, a widget on her home screen asks if she’s considered an emergency fund.

content.alt: Two iPhones with an arrow: a phone home screen with a Garden widget asking “Have you considered an emergency fund?”, then Garden’s home with the same suggestion in a green card at the top
content.caption: The widget, then the same nudge on Home.

content: On Home, the same suggestion sits at the top, based on her journey so far. A lock-screen notification can do the same: “Pssst... have you considered an emergency fund?”

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: Results and lessons
content: We presented Garden in a three-minute live pitch, told as Sarah’s story. It followed her from a $2,000 down payment that felt like a mountain to reaching her goal six months later, then two years on to an emergency fund. Alongside the pitch, we made a clickable prototype of the app.

bullets: **Pitch it as a story.** Following Sarah made the features make sense in three minutes.
**Make progress visible.** Flowers and trees make saving feel like progress, not just numbers.
